newsitem.title: UK: UK's Blair says will attend Hong Kong handover.
newsitem.headline: UK's Blair says will attend Hong Kong handover.

text.p: British Prime Minister Tony Blair ended weeks of speculation by confirming on Wednesday that he would attend a ceremony to mark the handover of Hong Kong to China at midnight on June 30.

There had been suggestions that Blair might stay away after China revealed it would use the festivities to swear in the unelected provisional legislature which will replace Hong Kong's parliament, democratically elected in 1995.
Officials made clear that although Blair would attend the formal handover ceremony he would leave before the swearing in started.

Blair, asked in parliament if Britain owed a moral duty to the people of Hong Kong which would not end with the handover, said: "I do agree...I think that is important...I will be attending the ceremony myself."
The Labour government, swept to power in an election landslide on May 1, has said it will continue to put pressure on Beijing to respect human rights in Hong Kong.
"For the prime minister, the paramount thing is to make clear Britain's commitment to Hong Kong now and in the future," a British official told reporters.
China earlier announced that President Jiang Zemin would attend the ceremony in the first visit to the territory -- a British colony for 156 years -- by a top Chinese leader.

The West has criticised Beijing for replacing the current parliament with the provisional legislature, whose 400 members were hand-picked by China in a move which effectively scrapped the colony's democratic reforms.
The United States said on Tuesday that Secretary of State Madeleine Albright would boycott the investiture of the unelected legislature.
But it remained to be seen whether Britain's other main partners, some of which have signed major trade deals with China, would follow suit.
Officials said Britain would raise the matter at a summit of European Union nations in Amsterdam next week and at a meeting of the Group of Seven industrialised nations in Denver later this month.
"We are explaining our position and hope they (our partners) take the same decision as us. We are not asking for a common European position," said the official.

"Other countries have interests in China and the right thing for us is to set out our position," he added, deflecting suggestions that Britain was not asking its partners for support in case they declined.
Britain has been arguing for months with China over details of the handover ceremony but concedes it can do little to prevent the new legislature being sworn in.
"We didn't think what was necessary. Normally the legislature would have been sworn in in its own building," said the official.
"You can see it as them making a point that they're there to stay and trying to get some legitimacy for the provisional legislature."
